text: László Moholy-Nagy's largest accomplishment may be the Institute of Design in Chicago, which survives today as part of the Illinois Institute of Technology and which art historian Elizabeth Siegel called his overarching work of art. He was born László Weisz in Bácsborsód, Hungary, to a Jewish family, and his father abandoned them early. He was a Hungarian painter and photographer and a professor at the Bauhaus. Constructivism influenced him strongly, and he advocated integrating technology and industry into the arts. He worked collaboratively with Lucia Moholy, Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer, among others.

Jan van Troyen is mainly known for his work for David Teniers the Younger on the illustrations for the Theatrum Pictorium, a publication that gave an overview of the paintings in the collection of Archduke Leopold Wilhelm. He accompanied Teniers to Vienna after the Archduke returned there in 1658, presumably to make engravings after paintings in the Archduke's cabinet for the 1673 edition. He is last recorded in Brussels in 1670. Most of his works are engravings of Italian paintings in the Archduke's cabinet. He was a Flemish engraver and etcher.

Federico de Madrazo y Kuntz belonged to a family that has been described as one of the most important painting dynasties, one that literally dominated 19th-century painting in Spain. He was born in Rome, the son of José de Madrazo, the painter and former Director of the Prado Museum. His children included the painters Ricardo and Raimundo and Cecilia, who married the Orientalist artist Marià Fortuny. He received his first instruction from his father. While still attending classes at the Royal Academy of San Fernando, he painted his first picture, The Resurrection of Christ, which Queen Christina bought in 1829.

Sakai Hōitsu painted in the Rinpa school and is known for having revived the style and popularity of Ogata Kōrin. He also made a number of reproductions of Kōrin's work. He was born in Edo in 1761, and his father was the lord, or daimyō, of Himeji Castle in Harima Province. The Sakai daimyō clan originated in Mikawa Province, and it claims descent from Minamoto no Arichika.

Carroll Beckwith, as he preferred to be known, painted landscapes, portraits and genre scenes in a Naturalist style that won him recognition as a respected figure in American art. He was born in Hannibal, Missouri, but grew up in Chicago, where his father started a wholesale grocery business. At sixteen he studied art at the Chicago Academy of Design under Walter Shirlaw, until the great fire of 1871 destroyed everything. He then went to New York and studied at the National Academy of Design. In 1873 he travelled to Paris, where he stayed until 1878.

Karl Ludwig Frommel was born at Birkenfeld and studied at Karlsruhe under Becker and Haldenwang. He visited Paris and earned a considerable reputation in Italy, where he stayed from 1812 for several years. He was appointed professor at Karlsruhe, where he founded the Society of Art and Industry. After a visit to London in 1824 to acquaint himself with the technique of steel engraving, he opened a studio with Henry Winkles in Karlsruhe for that branch of art. He later directed the picture gallery there for many years. He was the father of Emil Frommel.

Amaldus Nielsen lived most of his childhood and adolescence without a father, in the town of Mandal. He received some tuition from a travelling drawing teacher and went to Copenhagen to study in 1854. After a year of painting studies there he enrolled at the Academy of Art, but he failed to progress in the academy's system. With financial support from his brother and the business owner Diderik Cappelen, he studied under Hans Gude at the Düsseldorf Academy for two years. After that he spent four years travelling over Western and Southern Norway.

Nicolaas Pieneman specialised in paintings of recent history and in portraits. He was born in Amersfoort, the son of the painter Jan Willem Pieneman, and studied under his father and at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Amsterdam. He was also a pupil of Jean Baptiste Madou. A friend of William II of the Netherlands, he painted the king's inauguration in 1840 and many members of the royal family. In 1855 an oil portrait of King Willem III by Pieneman was presented in Japan, together with the steamship Soembing.

Albert Guillaume became a leading caricaturist during the Belle Époque. He was born in Paris and is remembered for his poster art, though he also painted in oils, such as Soirée parisienne, a portrait of Parisian dinner society. He created theater posters as well as advertising posters that were greatly influenced by the work of Jules Chéret. Guillaume thrived during the international poster mania of the Gay Nineties, when artists helped transform the boulevards of Paris into a gallery of fine art.

José Ferraz de Almeida Júnior was one of the first artists in Brazil to paint in the Realistic tradition of Gustave Courbet and Jean-François Millet. He was born in Itu, and his art career began while he was working as a bell-ringer at the local church. Some small works he made on religious themes impressed the head priest enough to hold a fundraising for him to go to Rio de Janeiro for formal art lessons. In 1869 he enrolled at the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts, where he studied with Victor Meirelles and Pedro Américo.

François Bonvin lost his mother to tuberculosis when he was four and was left in the care of an old woman who underfed him. His father soon married another seamstress and brought the boy back into the household. Nine more children were born, among them Léon Bonvin, who also became an artist. The family's resources were severely strained, and his stepmother abused and undernourished François. He grew up in humble circumstances in Paris and became a French realist painter.

Barthel Bruyn, usually called the Elder, was Cologne's foremost portrait painter of his day. He painted altarpieces as well as portraits, and he was a German Renaissance painter active in Cologne. He was born in Wesel or Cologne, and his early works suggest that he trained in the Lower Rhine. His earliest documented altarpiece is a Coronation of the Virgin, painted around 1515 for Doctor Peter von Clapis.

Hendrick ter Brugghen was one of the Utrecht Caravaggisti, the Dutch followers of Caravaggio. With Gerrit van Hondhorst and Dirck van Baburen, he was one of the most important Dutch painters influenced by Caravaggio. He painted genre scenes and religious subjects. No references to him written during his life have been identified. His father, Jan Egbertsz ter Brugghen, originally from Overijssel, had moved to Utrecht, where William the Silent appointed him secretary to the Court of Utrecht.

Thomas de Leu was the son of a print dealer in Oudenaarde and began his career in Antwerp, where he worked for Jean Ditmar and was influenced by the Wierix family. Sometime after 1576 and before 1580 he went to Paris to work for the painter and engraver Jean Rabel. He married Marie Caron, the daughter of Antoine Caron, one of the principal painters of the Second School of Fontainebleau, in 1583. He was a French engraver, publisher and print dealer of Flemish origin.

Jules Schmalzigaug came from a well-to-do family from Germany that lived in Antwerp. From the age of sixteen he travelled extensively. In 1905 he made a tour of Italy, where Venice especially impressed and influenced him. Back in Antwerp he became secretary of the art society Kunst van Heden and worked on the organisation of international exhibitions. Between 1910 and 1912 he lived mainly in Paris. He was a Belgian futurist painter, born in Antwerp, who died in The Hague.

Willem Kalf was one of the most prominent Dutch still-life painters of the 17th century. We first get acquainted with him through Arnold Houbraken, who speaks very highly of him. Kalf was a highly regarded and celebrated artist during his own lifetime, thanks to his extensive art knowledge and, according to Houbraken, his affable personality. His claim to fame now rests mostly on his mature still lifes, pronkstilleven in Dutch, which feature the most exotic and luxurious objects.

Edme Bouchardon is best known for his neoclassical statues in the gardens of Versailles and for the Fountain of Four Seasons in Paris. His equestrian statue of Louis XV for the Place de la Concorde was destroyed during the French Revolution. He was also a draftsman and painter, and he made celebrated series of engravings of working-class Parisians. He was born in Chaumont-en-Bassigny, the son of the sculptor and architect Jean-Baptiste Bouchardon. He learned sculpture first in his father's studio and then with Guillaume Coustou.

Thomas Herbert Maguire was a brilliant pupil of Richard James Lane, one of the favourite collaborators of the Swiss portrait painter Alfred Edward Chalon in the pages of the Illustrated London News. His series of 60 scientific portraits was privately commissioned by George Ransome of Ipswich, in connection with the founding of the Ipswich Museum. They were made between 1847 and 1852, as the museum obtained fresh scientific sponsors. Some were made from life, and others from photographic portraits or, in the case of the Revd William Kirby, from an oil portrait.

Sina Mesdag-van Houten was the wife of the marine painter Hendrik Willem Mesdag and a painter herself. She married him in 1856. She was the eldest of seven children, and one of her brothers later became Minister Samuel van Houten. She began to paint in 1871, after she lost her only child, the eight-year-old Klaas, and her husband and her cousin Lawrence Alma-Tadema helped her painting. She specialized in landscapes and still lifes but also painted portraits. In 1881 she took part in painting the Panorama Mesdag.

Antoine-Louis Barye worked as an animalier, a sculptor of animals, in the Romantic period. His son and student was the sculptor Alfred Barye. He was born in Paris. He began his career as a goldsmith, like many sculptors of the Romantic period. He first worked under his father Pierre, and around 1810 under Martin-Guillaume Biennais, a goldsmith to Napoleon. After studying under François-Joseph Bosio and the painter Baron Gros, he was admitted to the École des Beaux-Arts in 1818.

Willem de Famars Testas was noted for his Orientalist paintings and drawings. He was a Dutch painter, draughtsman, etcher and illustrator, born in Utrecht. According to the RKD, he learned to paint from Jacobus Everhardus Josephus van den Berg and studied at the academy in The Hague in 1853. He travelled to Egypt in 1858 and was in Brussels from 1872. He became a member of the artist society Kunstliefde in Utrecht. His daughter Marie Madelaine also became a painter.

Hiroshi Yoshida is regarded, along with Hasui Kawase, as one of the greatest artists of the shin-hanga style, and he is noted especially for his landscape prints. He made numerous trips around the world to get to know different artistic expressions and to make works of different landscapes. He was particularly known for his images of non-Japanese subjects done in traditional Japanese woodblock style, including the Taj Mahal, the Swiss Alps and the Grand Canyon. He was a 20th-century Japanese painter and woodblock printmaker.

Fra Bartolomeo spent all his career in Florence until his mid-forties, when he travelled to work in various cities, as far south as Rome. He was an Italian Renaissance painter of religious subjects, also known as Baccio della Porta, his original nickname. He belonged to the Dominican order. He trained with Cosimo Rosselli and in the 1490s fell under the influence of Savonarola.

François de Poilly got his first drawing lessons from his father, a goldsmith in Abbeville. He was apprenticed to the Parisian engraver Pierre Daret. Then he travelled to Rome, where he stayed for seven years with the engraver Cornelis Bloemaert and mastered the art. He is noted for approximately 400 engravings, mainly of religious subjects after Raphael, Guido Reni and Charles Le Brun, among others. He died in Paris.

Johann Baptist Reiter was an Austrian portrait and genre painter of the Biedermeier period, born in Linz. His father was a master carpenter, and Johann spent three years as an apprentice at his father's company, painting furniture, signs and crosses. Encouraged by the lithographer and art dealer Josef Hafner, he enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna. His teachers there included Leopold Kupelwieser and Thomas Ender. After 1830 he largely earned his living as a porcelain painter.

Alphonse Stengelin spent much of his life working outside France and is remembered mostly for his landscapes. He was born in a house designed by the architect Jacques-Germain Soufflot, who designed the Panthéon. His parents were Swiss, and his father was a banker. After studying at the Collège-lycée Ampère, he enrolled at the École des beaux-arts de Lyon and became a student of the school's director, Joseph Guichard. He also worked with the landscape painters Augustin Chenu and Florian-Némorin Cabane.

Frédéric Théodore Faber, a Belgian landscape and genre painter, was born in Brussels in 1782 and first instructed by his father. In 1799 he went to Antwerp and studied under Balthasar Paul Ommeganck. Afterwards he established a china manufactory in Brussels and abandoned painting on canvas for painting on porcelain. He also etched upwards of a hundred plates of landscapes and animals, some after his own designs and others after Ommeganck, De Roy and Van Assche. A significant set of his pieces is exhibited at the Museum of Decorative Arts François Duesberg in Mons.

Pieter Lastman is considered important as a painter of history pieces and because his pupils included Rembrandt and Jan Lievens. In his paintings he paid careful attention to the faces, hands and feet. He was born in Amsterdam, the fourth child of Pieter Segersz, a town beadle who was dismissed in 1578 for being a Catholic. His mother, Barber Jacobsdr, was an appraiser of paintings and goods. His apprenticeship was with Gerrit Pietersz Sweelinck, the brother of Jan Pieterszoon Sweelinck.

Robert Dighton founded a dynasty of artists who followed in his footsteps. He was an English portrait painter and printmaker, and also a caricaturist, and the son of the London printseller John Dighton. In the 1770s he began acting and singing in plays at the Haymarket Theatre, Covent Garden and Sadler's Wells, while at the same time training and exhibiting at the Royal Academy, whose school he entered in 1772. The first prints he designed were of actors for John Bell's edition of Shakespeare.

Anthonie Palamedesz, born Antonius Stevens in Leith, Scotland, is known in particular for his merry company paintings of elegant figures engaged in play, music and conversation, and for his guardroom scenes with soldiers. Like many Dutch painters of his time, he also painted portraits and still lifes, including vanitas still lifes. He further painted the staffage in a few views of the interior of churches. He helped develop genre painting in Delft in the mid 17th century.

Ferdinand Olivier belonged to a family of Swiss-French descent and became a German painter linked to the Nazarene movement. He began his artistic education in 1801 by taking drawing lessons from Carl Wilhelm Kolbe, and he also studied with the woodblock printers Christian Haldenwang and Johann Friedrich Unger. In 1804 he moved to Dresden with his brother Heinrich. There he studied with Jacob Wilhelm Mechau and Karl Ludwig Kaaz, copied old masters in the Gemäldegalerie, and got to know Caspar David Friedrich and Philipp Otto Runge.

Gerard David was an Early Netherlandish painter and manuscript illuminator known for his use of color. Only a bare outline of his life survives. He may have been the Meester gheraet van brugghe who became a master of the Antwerp guild in 1515. He was very successful in his lifetime and probably ran two workshops, in Antwerp and Bruges. Like many painters of his period, his reputation diminished in the 17th century until he was rediscovered in the 19th century. He was born in Oudewater, now in the province of Utrecht.

Hippolyte Bellangé was a French battle painter and printmaker whose art was influenced by the wars of the first Napoleon. While still a youth, he produced several military drawings in lithography. He afterwards pursued systematic studies under Gros and, with the exception of some portraits, devoted himself exclusively to battle pieces. In 1824 he received a second class medal for a historical picture, and in 1834 the decoration of the Legion of Honour. He also gained a prize at the Paris Universal Exhibition of 1855.

Domenico Quaglio the Younger was the second son of Giuseppe Quaglio and part of the large Quaglio family of Italian artists, who worked in architecture, indoor fresco decoration and scenography for the court theatres. He was known as a landscape and architectural painter and decorator, including quadratura. He was born in Munich, and his father taught him perspective and scene painting, while Mettenleiter and Karl Hess taught him engraving. In 1819 he resigned his post as scene painter and occupied himself only with architectural painting.

Georges Valmier's work took in the great movements of modern painting, starting with Impressionism in his early years, then Cubism, which he discovered when he was around 25, and finally Abstractionism from 1921. He also designed sets and costumes for theater and ballet and models for fabrics and carpets. His oil paintings do not exceed 300 in number, since he died prematurely at the age of 51. They were the culmination of many preparatory drafts in gouache.

James Peale is best known for his miniature and still life paintings. He was the younger brother of the noted painter Charles Willson Peale. He was born in Chestertown, Maryland. His father died when he was an infant, and the family moved to Annapolis. In 1762 he began apprenticeships there, first in a saddlery and later in a cabinetmaking shop. After Charles returned from studying with Benjamin West in London in 1769, James served as his assistant.

Henry Edridge was the son of a tradesman and was apprenticed at fifteen to the mezzotinter and landscapist William Pether. He became proficient as a painter of miniatures, portraits and landscapes. His first portraits were on ivory. He then turned to paper with black lead and India ink, adding very ornate backgrounds, and later produced a large number of elaborately finished pictures in water colours with light backgrounds. These were followed by others in which he combined the depth and richness of oil paintings with the freedom of water colour drawings.

Abraham Genoels, nicknamed Archimedes, is now mainly known for his landscape paintings and prints. He was a Flemish Baroque painter and engraver who had an international career, working in Paris, Rome and Antwerp. He was born in Antwerp. His father was the starch maker Peter Genoels and his mother was Cornelia Melis. From age eleven to fifteen he studied drawing under Jacques Backereel, and later perspective under Nicolaes Fierlants. He decided to leave Antwerp as soon as he had finished his studies.

Karel de Bazel became the first chairman of the Association of Dutch Architects in 1909, and Adriaan Frederik van der Weij was his student. He was a modern Dutch architect who also worked as an engraver and draftsman and designed furniture and carpets. He was born in Den Helder to Karel Pieter Cornelis de Bazel, caretaker of the Ministry of Marine, and Petronella Elisabeth Koch. He came from a modest background.

Serge Sudeikin was banned from the Moscow School of Painting, Sculpture and Architecture for his obscene drawings, and then he joined the Mir Iskusstva movement. He was a Russian artist and set designer who worked for the Ballets Russes and the Metropolitan Opera. He was born in Saint Petersburg in 1882 and died in Nyack, New York, in 1946. His close friends included the poet Mikhail Kuzmin and the impresario Serge Diaghilev, at whose invitation he came to Paris in 1906 for the Salon d'Automne, where his work was first shown abroad.

Theodor Hörmann von Hörbach began his career in the Austrian Army and served in the Second Italian War of Independence, followed by service in the Austro-Prussian War. He reached the rank of Oberleutnant. From 1873 to 1875 he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna with Eduard Peithner von Lichtenfels and Anselm Feuerbach. After that he taught drawing and fencing at the Military Realschule in Sankt Pölten. He lived in Paris from 1886, where he came under the influence of Impressionism. He later settled in Vienna and became a member of the Künstlerhaus.

François-André Vincent was the son of the miniaturist François-Elie Vincent and studied under Joseph-Marie Vien. He won the Prix de Rome and studied at the French Academy in Rome from 1771 to 1775. There he was installed at the Palais Mancini and painted numerous portraits inspired by the style of Jean-Honoré Fragonard. In 1790 he was appointed master of drawings to Louis XVI. He later became a professor at the Académie royale de peinture et de sculpture in Paris. He married the painter Adélaïde Labille-Guiard.

Fritz Boehle was the eldest of four brothers, and his mother ran a small haberdashery in their hometown of Emmendingen. He began his art education at the Städel Institute in Frankfurt, studying drawing under Heinrich Hasselhorst and painting under Johann Frank Kirchbach. At age 22 he went to Munich to study under Wilhelm von Diez. He greatly admired old masters such as Matthäus Merian the Elder and Wenceslaus Hollar. In 1897 he settled permanently in Sachsenhausen. He is best known for his realistic and romantic depictions of rural German life.

Arthur Devis was the eldest son of Anthony Devis, a carpenter and bookseller who became a freeman of Preston, Lancashire. The Flemish painter Peter Tillemans became his teacher. During the early 1730s he assisted in Tillemans's London studio, apparently copying views of Italy by artists such as Pannini and Marco Ricci. After moving to London he switched to portraiture and acquired a considerable reputation, although this success did not last. Unable to adapt to later fashionable artistic currents, his commissions declined.

Frédéric Bazille grew up on a wine-producing estate in Castelnau-le-Lez near Montpellier. He became interested in painting after seeing works by Eugène Delacroix. His family let him study painting only if he also studied medicine. In 1862 he moved to Paris to continue his medical studies, where he met Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Alfred Sisley and began taking classes in Charles Gleyre's studio. After failing his medical exam in 1864 he painted full-time. Many of his works place a figure within a landscape painted en plein air.

Frederik Hendrik Kaemmerer began his artistic studies at the Royal Academy of Art in The Hague with Salomon Verveer, who taught in the Romantic tradition. His early works were mostly landscapes in the style of the Hague School. In 1865 he went to Paris and enrolled at the Académie des Beaux-Arts, where he studied with Jean-Léon Gérôme and switched to a more Academic style. Inspired by the effects of sunlight on the water during stays in Scheveningen, he began his transition to Impressionism. He won a silver medal at the Exposition Universelle in 1889.

Henri de Braekeleer was trained in drawing by his father Ferdinand, a genre painter, and by his uncle Jan August Hendrik Leys. He entered the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Antwerp in 1854 and remained a student there until 1861. In 1863 he went to Germany and then to the Netherlands to study works by earlier painters. The influence of Johannes Vermeer was especially important. One of his characteristic subjects is a single person absorbed in a quiet activity, shown in an interior lit by a window.

Thomas Couture sold a sketch for one hundred francs as a child. At eleven he moved with his family to Paris, where he studied at the industrial arts school and later at the École des Beaux-Arts. He was a student of Baron Antoine Jean-Gros. He failed the Prix de Rome competition six times, but he felt the problem was with the École, not himself, and he finally won the prize in 1837. After the success of Romans During the Decadence in 1847, he opened an independent atelier meant to challenge the École.

Vicente López Portaña began formally studying painting in Valencia at thirteen as a disciple of father Antonio de Villanueva, a Franciscan friar. He also studied at the Academy of San Carlos in his native city. At seventeen he won first prize in drawing and coloring, which brought a scholarship to the Academia Real de Bellas Artes de San Fernando in Madrid. For three years there he apprenticed with the painter Mariano Salvador Maella. He later became vice-director of painting at the Academy of San Carlos. His sons Bernardo and Luis were also painters.

The working-class area of Etterbeek on the outskirts of Brussels was where Constantin Meunier was born. His family was poor, and his father committed suicide when he was four. He began studying sculpture at fourteen at the Academy of Fine Arts in Brussels and later attended the private studio of Charles-Auguste Fraikin. His encounter with Gustave Courbet's The Stone Breakers made him doubt that sculpture could represent the social issues that concerned him. He then turned to painting for the next thirty years. He is best known for realist depictions of agricultural labourers and coal miners.

François-Xavier Fabre trained at the art academy in Montpellier before joining the studio of Jacques-Louis David in Paris. His studies were paid for by the financier and art collector Philippe-Laurent de Joubert. During the French Revolution he went to live in Florence and became a member of the Florentine Academy, where he taught painting. He is said to have married Princess Louise of Stolberg-Gedern, the widow of the dramatist Vittorio Alfieri. On her death in 1824 he inherited her fortune and used it to found an art school in his home town. He bequeathed his collection to the town.

Claude Vignon received his initial artistic training in Paris from the Mannerist painter Jacob Bunel, a representative of the Second School of Fontainebleau. He likely travelled to Rome as early as 1609, where he formed part of the French community of painters that included Simon Vouet and Valentin de Boulogne. He returned to France in 1616 and became a member of the Painter's Guild of Paris that year. He also visited Spain, where he was reportedly attacked by eight bandits in Barcelona. He worked in many genres.

Huib Luns drew his early interest in art from a visit to the studios of Lawrence Alma-Tadema, a Dutch painter who lived in London. His first drawing lessons came from the brothers Antoon and Theo Molkenboer. He then attended a school for arts and crafts in Amsterdam and served an internship at the Rijksakademie. His first studio was in Brussels, where he worked with the Belgian sculptor Charles van der Stappen. In 1904 he entered the Prix de Rome competition, but his friend Jan Sluijters was the winner. He also designed book covers, posters and medals.

Educated in Florence by the painter and sculptor Andrea del Verrocchio, Leonardo da Vinci began his career in that city. He then spent much time in the service of Ludovico Sforza in Milan. Later he worked in Florence and Milan again, as well as briefly in Rome, attracting a large following of imitators and students. At the invitation of Francis I, he spent his last three years in France, where he died in 1519. His fame initially rested on his work as a painter, but he also kept notebooks with drawings and notes on subjects such as anatomy and astronomy.

John Webber was educated in Bern and studied painting in Paris. His father was Abraham Wäber, a Swiss sculptor who had moved to London. Webber served as official artist on James Cook's third voyage of discovery around the Pacific, and he became the first European artist to make contact with Hawaii, then called the Sandwich Islands. He made numerous watercolour landscapes of the islands of Kauai and Hawaii and also portrayed many of the Hawaiian people. His drawings and paintings were engraved for the British Admiralty's account of the expedition, published in 1784.

Karl von Blaas came from a peasant family at Nauders in the Tyrol. His first art lessons were in Innsbruck. His uncle, a judge in Verona, recognized his talent and gave him financial support for study in Venice, which he undertook in 1832. He studied at the Venice Academy under Lodovico Lipparini. In 1837 he received the Prix de Rome from the Venetian Academy, which allowed him to study in Rome for five years. There he met Friedrich Overbeck and his circle but disagreed with them artistically.

Prilidiano Pueyrredón was the only son of Juan Martín de Pueyrredón, then the Supreme Director of the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata. In 1835 his family relocated to Europe, where he spent the school year in Paris and summers in Cádiz. The family later left Europe for Rio de Janeiro, whose liberal atmosphere encouraged his artistic vocation. On his return to Paris three years later he received his parents' permission to study engineering. In 1849 the whole family returned to Buenos Aires.

Heywood Hardy was the youngest of ten children of the artist James Hardy senior. At seventeen he left the family home in Bath after an argument with his father and moved to Keynsham near Bristol. His first two paintings, both landscapes, were accepted for exhibition at the Royal Academy in 1864. Later that year he left Keynsham to study at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, where his principal teacher was Isidore Pils. He spent much of his spare time copying paintings in the Louvre.

Jan Asselijn came from a French Huguenot family in Dieppe and was originally named Jean Asselin. He received instruction from Esaias van de Velde and distinguished himself in landscape and animal painting. He traveled in France and Italy and modeled his style after Pieter van Laer, known as Bamboccio. In 1645 he married one of two sisters from Antwerp in Lyons, and Nicolaes de Helt Stockade married the other. Asselijn had a withered hand and was small of stature, which earned him the nickname Krabbetje, meaning little claw, among the Bentvueghels.

Utagawa Toyohiro studied under Utagawa Toyoharu, the founder of the Utagawa school, and entered his studio in 1782 together with his contemporary Toyokuni. Toyoharu gave him the name Toyohiro and allowed him to use the gō Ichiryūsai. His works include a number of ukiyo-e landscape series and many depictions of the daily activities in the Yoshiwara entertainment quarter. He also produced a series of ukiyo-e triptychs in collaboration with Toyokuni. Hiroshige studied under him.

Max Rosenthal studied in Berlin under Professor Carl Harnisch. He then went to Paris, where he studied lithography with Martin Thurwanger, with whom he came to Philadelphia in 1849. He made the chromolithographic plates for what is believed to be the first fully illustrated book by this process in the United States. In 1854 he lithographed an interior view of the old Masonic temple in Philadelphia, the largest chromolithograph made in the country up to that time. During the Civil War he followed the Army of the Potomac and drew every camp.

Pieter de Molijn was baptized in the Dutch Reformed Austin Friars church in London, the son of Pieter de Moijn from Ghent and Lynken van den Bossche from Brussels. Little is known of his early training, but he probably traveled to Italy and in 1616 he became a member of the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke. He lived in Delft from 1616 to 1627, where he remarried after his first wife died. He taught several students, including Allart van Everdingen. He was known for his landscapes, but he also made genre pieces and marine scenes.

Antoine Coypel studied under his father Noël Coypel, with whom he spent four years in Rome after his father had been appointed director of the French academy in 1672. In Rome he sketched the Antique monuments and studied the works of the Italian Renaissance and Baroque. He became acquainted with Gianlorenzo Bernini, who became his mentor. He won a prize for drawing at the Accademia di San Luca. He became court painter first to Philippe I, Duke of Orléans, and later to King Louis XV. He became director of the Académie Royale.

Jacob van der Ulft was the son of the mayor of Gorinchem. Like his father, he became mayor of Gorinchem and held the office until 1679. That year he fled to The Hague for a short period following accusations of corruption. In 1683 he left Gorinchem for good and moved to Noordwijk, where he later died. He was known for his architectural and city views, landscapes and topographical views. He also worked as a glass painter.

William Sidney Mount spent much of his life in Setauket on Long Island and the adjacent village of Stony Brook, where he painted portraits, landscapes and scenes inspired by daily life. He chronicled rural life on Long Island and was the first native-born American artist to specialize in genre painting. His parents operated a farm, as well as a store and tavern on the village green. He also played the fiddle and composed, and he designed and patented several versions of his own violin, which he named the Cradle of Harmony. Many of his paintings feature musicians.

Alonso Cano learned architecture from his father Miguel Cano and sculpture from Juan Martínez Montañés. He studied painting in the academy of Juan del Castillo and with Francisco Pacheco, the teacher of Velázquez. He was made first royal architect and painter to Philip IV, and he also worked as instructor to the prince Balthasar Charles. The king gave him the post of canon of Granada Cathedral in 1652, so that he could take up the position of chief architect there. Toward the end of his life he designed its façade, which was erected after his death.

Frans van den Wyngaerde came from a family of fishmongers and was baptized in Antwerp in July. He became an apprentice of the Rubens collaborator Paulus Pontius when he was about 14 years old. He enrolled as a master in the Antwerp painters' guild, and the dean loaned him part of the membership fee because he lacked funds. In 1640 he married Maria Cruyt, the daughter of wealthy merchants, and became a captain of a local civil guard. By the middle of the 17th century he was a leading publisher of prints in Antwerp. He died in 1679.

Henri Leys was the son of a printer who specialized in religious images printed from old copper plates. His first etching was a funeral image made for his father's shop in 1831. He was keen on drawing, and his parents let him study under a furniture painter who lived next door. He then studied at the Antwerp Academy of Fine Arts under Mattheus Ignatius van Bree, among others. He worked in the studio of his brother-in-law, the genre painter Ferdinand de Braekeleer. He pioneered Belgian Realism.

George Caleb Bingham was known in his lifetime as the Missouri artist. His paintings chronicle America's westward expansion and depict life along the Mississippi and Missouri rivers before the steamboat era. His Fur Traders Descending the Missouri, painted in 1845, is held by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. He also produced as many as 500 portraits, depicting Missouri pioneers and politicians as well as John Quincy Adams and Senator Daniel Webster. A public electronic catalogue raisonné launched in 2018 compiles all of his known paintings.

Gerardus Emaus de Micault was the son of Pieter Emaus de Micault, who came from Dordrecht. By profession he was a tax collector, but he also left an extensive body of work as a draughtsman and etcher. He worked successively in The Hague, Lochem, Culemborg and Gouda. As an etcher and draughtsman he was a pupil of the officer and painter Ernst Willem Jan Bagelaar. He became best known for his soldier scenes and horse studies, as well as landscapes. In 1847 he published a study of amulets illustrated with his own lithographs.

Adolf Chwala was the son of a hatter and studied painting at the Academy of Fine Arts in Prague from 1851. He then studied landscape painting with Maximilian Joseph Haushofer. In 1864 he moved to Vienna, where he married Josefa Procházková. He had eight children, of whom Fritz and Leopoldine Emilie showed a talent for painting and received their first lessons in his studio. He was a member of the Vienna Künstlerhaus for thirteen years.

Alexander Ritter von Bensa turned to painting as a self-taught artist only later in life. Although he had not studied at the Vienna Academy, he was popular with clients from the court nobility and the upper middle class. He painted a series of scenes from war life, which won recognition and high prices. Archduke Joseph Ferdinand bought the Retreat from Königgrätz and the Skirmish at Schweinschädel, and Emperor Franz Joseph I bought numerous other paintings. The Battle of Tannenberg came into the possession of Archduke Wilhelm.

Zoltán Palugyay came from an old Hungarian family. After finishing secondary school in 1916 he was called up to the Italian front in the First World War, where he began his painting career as a soldier of the Austro-Hungarian army. After the war he studied at the art academies of Budapest and Kraków, and later at the private school of Hans Hofmann in Munich until 1926. He then returned to Slovakia to the family manor at Bodice, near Liptovský Mikuláš. He is called the founder of modern Slovak painting.

Johann Adam Delsenbach completed a three-year apprenticeship with the portrait engraver Augustin Fleischmann and attended the Nuremberg painters' academy. He travelled to Vienna in 1710, where Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach had called him to engrave the plates for his large architectural work. When the plague broke out there he returned to Nuremberg. In 1718 he went to Vienna again to make illustrations for a medal book commissioned by Carl Gustav Heraeus. That year Anton Florian, Prince of Liechtenstein, named him court engraver.

Friedrich Salathé was the son of the farmer Joseph Salathé and Eva Gysin. He became a pupil of Peter Birmann in Basel and moved to Rome in 1815 with Birmann's son Samuel and Jakob Christoph Bischoff. He served for some time in the papal guard. Bandits abducted him in 1819, and he was freed after six days. He later settled in Basel, where he devoted himself to watercolour painting and copper engraving. In 1823 he moved to Paris and stayed there for the rest of his life.

Nicolaes van Geelkercken was a land surveyor and cartographer in the service of the Gelderland government in the 17th century. He is known for his many manuscript maps, a large part of which are kept in the Gelders Archief. His sons Isaac, Jacob and Arnold van Geelkercken succeeded him in his trade. His brother Arnoldus was also a cartographer. He was born in Scherpenzeel around 1585 and died in Arnhem in 1656.

Johann Christian Klengel attended the drawing school in Dresden, where his teacher was Christian Wilhelm Ernst Dietrich. He went to Italy and in 1800 became a professor at the Dresden Art Academy. Karl Gottfried Traugott Faber was one of his pupils. He painted ideal landscapes and idyllic compositions, mostly in morning or evening light. In 1812 he published a collection of twelve folio sheets for landscape draughtsmen titled Principes de dessins pour les paysages, and in 1824 a similar number now known as Études de paysages.

Active between 1780 and 1796, Richard de Lalonde made numerous drawings and sketches, most of them engraved by Augustin Nicolas Foin and published by Jacques-François Chéreau. He also designed furniture with cabinetmakers such as Guillaume Beneman and Joseph Stöckel. Lalonde published a series of notebooks from 1780 called Cahiers de meubles, covering a very wide field of designs for interior decoration. His figures stress the decorated parts and use varied geometric forms softened into light ornaments such as rosettes, lyres, arcs and wreathed crowns.

Leopold Munsch was the son of a hotelier and worked from 1853 to 1867 as an official in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He took private drawing lessons in the 1840s. He attended evening painting courses with Peter Johann Nepomuk Geiger. He was influenced by the Viennese landscape painters Anton Hansch, Joseph Holzer and Remigius Adrianus Haanen. He mostly painted motifs from the mountain landscapes of South Tyrol and the Salzkammergut. He left more than 200 oil paintings and watercolours and over 2000 drawings.

Harmen ter Borch was the son of Gerard ter Borch the Elder and the younger brother of Gerard ter Borch the Younger, and he learned drawing from his father. Until the age of sixteen he drew genre scenes of good quality, above all of children and soldiers. In 1661 he gave up his artistic work because he took over his father's offices in Zwolle, or part of them. He was baptized in Zwolle in 1638 and died there before September 1677.

Oskar Mulley was the son of an official of the Carinthian savings bank. His drawing teacher at the state Realschule in Klagenfurt discovered his talent for painting when he was ten years old. He studied for a year in Munich at the painting school of the municipal trade school. From 1910 to 1913 he studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna under Alois Delug. He is counted among the representatives of Tyrolean art of the interwar period, and he became known above all for his paintings of mountain landscapes.

Georg Philipp Winterwerb grew up in Braubach and was meant to become a teacher at a seminary in Idstein. He left the seminary and began an apprenticeship at a lithographic institute in Mainz. He then moved to the lithographic institute of Carl Christian Otto Naumann in Frankfurt am Main, and alongside his work there as an engraver he attended the Städel Institute from 1846 under Jakob Becker and Edward Steinle. His first paintings recalled the Romantic painting of the Düsseldorf school. Recognition came in portraiture.

Alfred Henry Forrester was the son of a London public notary and followed his father's profession until 1839. He showed an aptitude for literary and artistic pursuits from an early age and wrote for periodicals such as Punch. He also drew on wood and made etchings and caricatures in pen and ink, specialising in anthropomorphic animals. Working as Alfred Crowquill, he published Phantasmagoria of Fun in two volumes in 1843. He also made popular ceramics, including a statuette of Wellington Bear. He was buried at West Norwood Cemetery.

The youngest of four children, Michel-Jean Cazabon grew up on Corinth Estate in northern Naparima, Trinidad, where his parents owned a sugar plantation. They were free colored immigrants from Martinique. In 1826 he went to school at Saint Edmund's College in Ware, England. He later sailed for Paris to study medicine but gave up these studies and became an art student under Paul Delaroche. He traveled extensively in France and Italy painting the landscape, and his work was shown at the Salon du Louvre in 1839.

Pierre Mignard was the younger brother of the painter and etcher Nicolas Mignard. He trained in Bourges with Jean Boucher and then studied with Simon Vouet. In 1635 he left for Rome and stayed about 22 years, painting many images of the Madonna and Child. He was summoned to Paris in 1657, probably by Cardinal Mazarin. There he painted portraits for Louis XIV and became a rival of Charles Le Brun, the first painter to the King. After Le Brun's death in 1690 he succeeded him as director of the academy.

Zéphirin Belliard, the Marseille-born son of a goldsmith, enrolled at the school of fine arts in Paris in 1817 and studied notably under Augustin Aubert and Paulin Guérin. He exhibited at the Paris Salon from 1822 to 1843. He worked mainly as a lithographer of portraits of public figures, copying paintings made by other artists. Honoré Daumier, whose father was a friend of Belliard, discovered lithography in his Marseille studio.
